name: DAMIC
notes: Two INSPIRE experiment records exist: the original Fermilab prototype (recid 1108203, FNAL-T-0987, approved 2008-12-15, completed 2012-04-09) and the current SNOLAB programme (recid 1401315). Both are represented as one experiment:damic record with dated intervals, per the same reasoning used for CDMS-II/SuperCDMS. external.inspire_experiment cites the current (SNOLAB) recid.

Status is recorded as `active`, not `completed`: the wave-3 brief describes DAMIC as completed (superseded by DAMIC-M), but no source fetched this session states an end date or an explicit cessation of DAMIC operations - the most recent DAMIC-specific paper found (INSPIRE literature 2752302, 2024-01) describes an active skipper-CCD run. This is flagged as an open item in the worklog rather than asserting the brief's claim without a citation (A17).

physics_goals.quote: our data exclude spin-independent WIMP-nucleon scattering cross sections as low as 3x10^-41 cm^2 for WIMPs with masses from 7 to 10 GeV/c^2
value: Search for WIMP and light dark matter via ionization signals in silicon CCDs

summary.plain: DAMIC searches for dark matter using the same kind of light-sensing chips found in digital cameras, cooled and shielded deep underground at SNOLAB in Canada. It started at Fermilab and moved to SNOLAB, later gaining even more sensitive 'skipper' chips.
summary.technical: Silicon CCD dark matter search; began as a shallow Fermilab prototype (2008-2012), then operated a tower of seven 16-Mpixel CCDs (~42 g, 11 kg-day exposure) at SNOLAB in 2017-2018, and later two 24-Mpixel skipper CCDs investigating a low-energy ionization excess through at least January 2024. Superseded in name by DAMIC-M at Modane, though no source fetched this session states DAMIC's own operations have formally ended.

unique_capabilities.quote: two silicon charge-coupled devices (CCDs), each with 24 megapixels and skipper readout, deployed in the DAMIC setup at SNOLAB
value: Thick, fully-depleted scientific CCDs with very low dark current, later upgraded to skipper-readout CCDs for single-electron sensitivity
